# S1MPA-1 Semester 1 Midterm review: Rome, Sasanian, Islam, Africa

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm (PA) History H review guide (PA). Writers: Althea Yang 9(9), Cynthia Chen 9(12). Editor: Bella Li 9(6). Range: Rome, Sasanian, Islam, Africa. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

Roman Empire

Before the Roman Empire:

- Punic wars
- Late Republic trends: expanded citizenship, required taxes and military service, huge wealth gap

Julius Caesar: Part of the First Triumvirate

- Civil war against Pompey (victory)
- Murdered by a group of Senators
- Reforms included creating the Julius calendar, expanding citizenship, distributing land to the poor, and public works to reduce unemployment

Augustus (Octavian): Part of the Second Triumvirate

- Adopted son of Julius Caesar
- Civil war against Marc Antony and Cleopatra
- Became the first emperor of the Roman Empire

After Augustus, emperors usually adopted an heir, with military holding large power

Tiberius: Stepson of Augustus, abolished assembly and extended northern frontier Caligula: Tiberius’s adopted son, 2 good and 2 bad years

Claudius: Uncle of Caligula, added Britannica, opened senate to provincials Nero: Blamed fire on Christians

Time of the Five Good Emperors → Pax Romana

Nerva: Adopts Trajan, empire at greatest extent under his rule

Hadrian: strengthened defenses, official start of Jewish Diaspora

Antonius Pius: worked to enfranchise free slaves

Marcus Aurelius: Wrote the Meditations, stoic philosopher, fought border wars and expanded trade links with China

Pax Romana: “Roman Peace”

- Controlled entire Mediterranean, almost no warfare
- Lasted around 200 years
- Increased citizenship

Third Century Crisis:

-   26 emperors in 50 years
- Extreme political instability

- Barbarian invasion, civil war, rebellion
- Debasement of currency/ economy weakened
- Plague, famine and disaster

4th century Rome:

Diocletian: saved the empire from third century crisis, divide empire into 4 administrative realms, last persecution of Christians

Constantine: legalized Christianity, move capital to Constantinople

Theodosius: last to rule whole empire, made Christianity official religion

Decline:

- widespread corruption àarmies decided emperors
- Eastern empire was richer and had more power
- Decline in traditional values
- Conflicts such as sack of Rome and Battle of Adrianople
- Slowly lose grasp on Britain

Odoacer captured Rome and deposed Romulus AugustulusàEnd of Western Roman Empire

China:

Qin unificationàstandardized writing, weights, measures etc.

- Heavy taxation, forced labor, and severe punishments lead to rebellion 206BCE: Gaozu emerged from civil wars and founded Han dynasty, govern more practically

Han Dynasty:

- Bureaucracy under emperor
- Social structure: mostly farmers (indebted), Confucianism made scholars, officials and cultivates above merchants, women in high status expected to obey, lower status women has more freedom

Emperor Wu: strengthened central authority, campaign against the Huns, connect silk roads Wang Mang seized the throne and founded the Xin Dynasty, restored under Guangwu

- Court struggles intensified competition
- Yellow Turban Rebellion: demand fairer treatment and redistribution of land Collapse: (189-220)
- struggle in court factions exploded into violence, central authority collapsed
- period of the Three Kingdoms started

Sasanian Dynasty:

Ardashir: defeats Parthian King Artabanus IV, founded the Sasanian Dynasty, titled “shahanshah”, king of kings

Shapur I: expanded empire east, repeatedly fought Rome

-     260CE: Captured Emperor Valerian at Battle of Edessa

Rome Sasanian wars continued, and neither side eliminated the otherà constant warfare Culture, cities and trade:

- Ctesiphon: major urban center
- Trade: Link to sink road
- Coins spread royal imagery
- Court culture and ideas influenced later empires

Khosrow I:

- Rebuilt royal power under an unstable state
- Tax reforms, organized military, broadened court elite, restrain noble independence Khosrow II:
- Last period of greatness for the Sasanian Empire
- Byzantine Emperor Heraclius launched a counterattack after Khosrow II invaded the Byzantine Empire

Collapse:

- Royals, nobles and generals fought for control after 628
- War with Rome and plague drained economy and manpower
- Central authority collapse
- Loss of Iraq to Arab Muslims
-     651: Yazdegerd III’s death marked the end of the Sasanian Dynasty

Religion:

Judaism:

- Messiah: the anointed one to lift Jews into greatness and spread worship
- Torah: Holy book of Judaism
- Talmud: interpretation of Jewish law
- Abraham: father of many nations

Christianity:

- Begins with Jesus, a Jewish teacher that performed miracles
- Crucified by romans in 34CE, resurrected
- His followers spread his message and religion and descendants wrote the 4 gospels

on the life of Jesus in the New Testament

Christians and Jews were facing religious tension during the period around Nero’s rule, and the Jewish started the first Jewish revolt.

Second Jewish revolt occurred during Hadrian’s rule

Confucianism:

- Made official state ideology in the Han dynasty
- System for choosing officials, people had to study Confucian classics
- Moral code for how people should behave

Zoroastrianism:

- Kingsàdefenders of order
- Religious law grew more organized

The Spread of Islam

The Origins of Islam

Before Muhammad

- Arabs are Semitic-speaking people originating from Southwestern Asia
- Islam is an Abrahamic, monotheistic religion, sharing a religious connection to Abraham with Judaism and Christianity
- The central region of Arab civilization is the Arabian Peninsula
- The region was originally inhabited by the Bedouin, whose religious practices involved the spirituality of objects and the worship of multiple gods, with Allah as the chief deity
- The Ka'aba is a sacred shrine in Mecca, traditionally associated with a sacred black stone. Before Muhammad, it was visited by people of different faiths
- Mecca was an important trading center on the Arabian Peninsula and the location of the Ka'aba

Muhammad

- Born into a wealthy family, Muhammad lived in Mecca and worked as a merchant for many years
- He became concerned about the differences in values between the Bedouins and the wealthy merchant class

- In 610 CE, he received his first revelation from Allah and began preaching his religious teachings
- The Qur'an was revealed to him over approximately two decades
- As he preached, he faced opposition and was eventually forced to leave Mecca
- Why?
- His teachings of monotheism threatened the existing religious and political order
- Merchants feared that discouraging the worship of other gods would reduce the number of pilgrims and traders visiting Mecca
- In 622 CE, Muhammad migrated to Medina. This migration is known as the Hijra (Hegira)
- With the support of the Bedouins, he established the first Muslim community, known as the Umma
- In 630 CE, Muhammad led a military force that captured Mecca

Islamic Religious Texts

Qur'an

- The central religious text of Islam; contains religious teachings, ethics, and guidance on law

Hadith

- A collection of the sayings and actions of Muhammad

Tafsir

- Interpretations and explanations of the Qur'an (exegesis)

Sira:

- Biographical accounts of Muhammad's life

5 Pillars of Islamic Belief

Shahada – The Creed

- Declaration of faith: "There is no God but Allah, and Muhammad is His Prophet"

Salat – The Prayers

- Muslims are obligated to pray five times a day: Fajr, Zuhr, Asr, Maghrib, and Isha

Sawm – The Fasting

- Fasting from dawn to sunset during the month of Ramadan

Hajj – The Pilgrimage

- Traveling to Mecca at least once in one's lifetime, if physically and financially able

Zakat – The Almsgiving

- Giving a portion of one's wealth to charity

Rashidun Caliphate

Definitions

- Caliph: the political leader of the religious community
- Caliphate: a dynasty of Islamic caliphs

Establishment

- Muhammad died in 632 CE without explicitly naming a successor
- A major debate over succession emerged between:
- Abu Bakr: Muhammad's father-in-law
- Ali: Muhammad's son-in-law and cousin
- This disagreement eventually contributed to the Sunni-Shia split:
- Sunnis supported Abu Bakr's succession
- Shias believed Ali should have succeeded Muhammad
- Abu Bakr was eventually appointed the first caliph, establishing the Rashidun Caliphate

The Four Caliphs

- The Rashidun Caliphate was ruled by four caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali
- Ali eventually became caliph but was assassinated in 661 CE
- Today, approximately 85% of Muslims are Sunni Muslims

Military Expansion

- Under the Rashidun Caliphate, Arab forces became a powerful, unified military force
- They began expanding into neighboring territories

- 636 CE: Defeated the Byzantine army at the Battle of Yarmouk
- 640s CE: Conquered Cairo from the Byzantine Empire
- 651 CE: Conquered the Sasanian Empire
- Later expansion: Continued conquests across North Africa
- Impact:
- Significantly weakened the Byzantine Empire
- Expanded Islamic political and military influence

Treatment of Non-Muslims

- Dhimmi: Non-Muslims, particularly Jews and Christians, who lived under Muslim rule and received protected status
- Jizya: A tax imposed on non-Muslims who did not convert to Islam
- The People of the Book (Jews and Christians) were granted certain protections in exchange for paying jizya

Umayyad Caliphate

Establishment

- Following Ali's assassination, Mu'awiya took power
- He moved the capital to Damascus and established the Umayyad Caliphate

Expansion

- Continued Islamic expansion across: The Mediterranean, Spain, North Africa
- The Battle of Tours (732 CE) marked a turning point in Arab expansion into Western Europe

- Umayyad forces confronted the Frankish military

Decline

- Several factors contributed to the eventual decline of the Umayyad Caliphate:
- Religious divisions (particularly the Shi’ite Schism)
- Bureaucratic corruption and excessive spending
- Decentralization of political power
- Growing resentment and rebellions in conquered territories

Abbasid Caliphate (750–1258 CE)

Establishment

- The Umayyads were overthrown by Abu al-Abbas, who established the Abbasid Caliphate
- The capital was moved to Baghdad

Political and Social Changes

- Baghdad became a major center of trade and urbanization
- The Abbasids introduced new governmental structures
- Society experienced significant changes, including
- Greater equality between Arab-born Muslims and converts
- Increased intermarriage
- Greater cultural exchange

Harun al-Rashid

- One of the most influential caliphs during the Abbasid Golden Age
- Supported scholarship, science, and cultural development
- Encouraged communication and exchange between different region
- Presided over a period of economic prosperity
- Helped establish Baghdad as a major center of knowledge
- Associated with the development of the House of Wisdom

Decline

- Political power gradually became decentralized.

- The vizier (prime minister) increasingly gained influence over the caliph.
- Extravagance and corruption weakened the government.
- The growing influence of the Seljuk Turks contributed to the decline of Abbasid political authority.

The Islamic Golden Age (750-1350)

- Dramatic growth in:
- Trade and commerce (assimilation with different cultures, including Greek, Persian, Indian, etc.)
- Science, mathematics, and medicine (Indo-Arabic numerals
- Flexibility in the social structure (people could work their way up the social ranks)
- Schools and libraries

The Byzantine Empire

Justinian

Rise to Power

- Emperor Justinian took the Byzantine throne in 527 CE
- Attempted to restore the imperial power of the former Western Roman Empire throughout the Mediterranean
- Established the Justinian Code, a major collection and organization of Roman laws
- Ruled alongside his wife, Empress Theodora

Economic Policies

- Established a strong imperial economy through heavy taxation, which placed a significant burden on poorer populations
- Taxes also helped fund the military and imperial expansion

The Nika Revolt (532 CE)

- A major rebellion in Constantinople involving two rival chariot-racing factions: Greens and Blues
- The revolt was fueled by political tensions and resentment over high taxes
- Burned large parts of Constantinople

- Following the revolt, Justinian rebuilt the Hippodrome, the center of chariot racing

Byzantine Politics

Military and Taxation

- Taxes were directed toward funding the military
- Despite these efforts, the Byzantine Empire gradually lost territories over the following centuries

Political Structure

- Emperor: The head of the empire, with authority over government and court rituals
- Bureaucracy: An administrative system composed of highly educated scholars and officials
- Provincial Governors: Responsible for managing local affairs

Byzantine Cultural Shifts

Cultural Influences

- Byzantine culture combined Hellenistic influences (Greek traditions and culture) with Orthodox Christian values
- Cultural diversity was reflected in: mosaics, architecture, language and writing systems

Changes Within the Church

- A patriarch was appointed to lead the Church (as opposed to the Pope)
- Significant value differences between the Pope and the Patriarch led to the Great Schism in 1054, separating the Orthodox Church from the Roman Church

Spread of Islam to the Swahili Coast

Swahili Shifts

Economic Changes

- Indian Ocean trade led to the growth of wealthy coastal city-states
- Trading ports became important centers of international commerce

Cultural Changes

- Trade and migration contributed to the spread of Islam
- Blending of African and foreign traditions created a distinct Swahili culture
- Syncretism: The blending of different religions and cultural traditions to create new beliefs, customs, and practices

Political Changes

- Independent city-states developed around important trading ports
- Political authority balanced local leadership with foreign commercial influence

Kilwa

Economic Importance

- Became a principal port for international trade in the Indian Ocean.
- Trade routes developed along the Swahili Coast, connecting important ports Mogadishu and Kilwa

Architecture

- Maritime causeways, mosques, distinctively Swahili warehouses

Foreign Visitors

- Visited by the Arab traveler Ibn Battuta in 1331
- Later visited by Portuguese explorers

Zimbabwe Before Islamic Influence

Religious and Cultural Beliefs

- Bantu-speaking peoples
- Animistic religious beliefs, involving spirituality in natural objects and elements

Social Organization

- Kinship-based societies
- Descent and inheritance could follow paternal or matrilineal lines

- Power-sharing systems existed in some societies, with authority distributed among different members rather than concentrated in a single ruler

Great Zimbabwe

Social Hierarchy

- Social stratification was reflected in the city's physical layout
- Higher social classes occupied areas at higher elevations
- Demonstrated differences in social status and wealth

Architecture and Engineering

- Advanced architectural knowledge, expertise, and access to resources enabled the construction of large stone walls.
- Demonstrated the society's engineering skills and organizational abilities

Trade and Economic Connections

- Fragments of Chinese porcelain were discovered at the site
- Evidence of participation in long-distance international trade networks

Art and Craftsmanship

- Stone statues demonstrated the craftsmanship and artistic abilities of local artisans
- Artwork reflected aspects of the society's kinship-based organization.

# S1F-1 Semester 1 Final review: The Rise of Islam, African Civilizations, Medieval Ages

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Final History H review guide (PA). Writers: Sunny Jin 9-1, Caitlin Zhou 9-2. Editor: Caitlin Zhou 9-2. Range: The Rise of Islam, African Civilizations, Medieval Ages. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Islam**

**Doctrine**

- **Monotheistic**; only worships one God, **Allah**
- **Muhammad** is his **Prophet**
- **Major Texts**
  - **The Quran**:
    - the holy Scriptures of Islam
    - “recitation”, also spelled “Koran”
    - believed to originate from Allah’s revelations to Muhammad, later dictated to scribes
  - **The Tafsir**: Exegesis (explanation/commentary) of the Quran
  - **The Hadith**: a collection of sayings and practices of Muhammad, the Prophet
  - **The Sira**: a biography of Muhammad
- **Five Pillars of Islam**
  - **Confession of Faith**: uncompromised monotheistic belief in Allah as the only god and Muhammad as his prophet
  - **Pray**: standard prayers facing Mecca five times a day and public prayers on Fridays at midday
  - **Fast**: to fast from dawn till sunset during the holy month of **Ramadan**, which commemorates Muhammad’s first revelation
  - **Charity**: to give alms, or zakat, to the poor and unfortunate, to demonstrate social responsibility
  - **Pilgrimage (hajj)**: if possible, to make a pilgrimage to Mecca to worship at the Kaaba at least once in a lifetime
- **Jihad**: “striving in the way of the Lord”
  - Jihad of the **tongue/pen**, **heart**, and **sword**

**The** **Founding of Islam**

**Pre-Islamic Arabia**

- Converted into a **Roman** Province (106 B.C.E.)
- The **Bedouin Arabs**
  - A **Semitic**-speaking people of Southwestern Asia
  - Tribal society
    - Each tribe was ruled by the **sheikh**, selected by a council of elders, the **majlis**
  - participated in the caravan trade and actively initiated trade between the **Persian Gulf** and the **Mediterranean Sea**
- **Pre-Islamic Religion**
  - **Polytheistic**, with a supreme deity, **Allah**
  - A communal faith
  - **Animistic** beliefs: spirits embodied natural entities
  - Allah was symbolized by a sacred stone
  - By the time of **Muhammad**, the **Kaaba**, located in **Mecca**, was held in special religious reverence
- The **economic significance** of Arabia increases (5th & 6th century C.E.), benefiting from the instability in Mesopotamia, etc.
- Consequence of the intensified trade, relations between the desert **Bedouins** and the wealthy **merchants** in town become **strained**

**Muhammad (570-632 C.E.)**

- **Early Life & Revelations** **(570-610 C.E.)**
  - Born into the **Quraysh** tribe; orphaned at an early age
  - Became a **merchant** in **Mecca**; married a wealthy widow, Khadijah
  - Was troubled by the widening gap between Bedouin values and the corruption of commercial elites
  - Allegedly received his **first revelation** from God (**610 C.E.**)
- **Founder of Islam** **(610-622 C.E.)**
  - Began to **preach Islam**; gained followers in Mecca
  - Kicked out by the leaders of Mecca **(622 C.E.)**
- **The Hijra/Hegira (622-632** **C.E.)**
  - Fled with family and followers to **Medina**
  - Formed the first Muslim community—the **umma**
  - Gathering an army, he returned to and **conquered** Mecca
  - Destroyed the **idols** of the traditional faith
  - Led prayer at the **Kaaba**, converting the city to Islam.

**The Sunni-Shi’a Split (632-680 C.E.)**

- Muhammad dies without naming a successor (632 C.E.)
- The **Caliph**-**successor**; **political** leader of the umma; an **imam**, or **religious** leader
  - **Ali**:
    - Muhammad’s cousin & son-in-law
    - Deemed too young
  - **Abu Bakr**
    - Muhammad’s father-in-law & close friend
    - Understood the politics of the region & the tribes
- **Abu Bakr** named Caliph (632-634 C.E.)
  - Loosely controlled warriors
  - **United** all Bedouin **Arab tribes**
  - Commenced **expansion** of Islam
- The **Rashidan** (or Rightly Guided Caliphs) (632-661 C.E.)
  - **Abu Bakr**, **Umar**, **Uthman**, **Ali**
- 3rd Caliph Uthman murdered**;** Ali’s supporters named him Caliph (656 C.E.)
- War erupts between Uthman’s & Ali’s supporters (657 C.E.)
- The **Umayyads** (an opposing family to Ali) declare their own Caliph in Jerusalem (660 C.E.)
- **Ali** is **assassinated** (661 C.E.); his sons are later killed in battle (680 C.E.)
- **The Sunni faith**
  - Muhammad cannot be **succeeded as prophet**
  - Abu Bakr was the best choice to be Caliph
  - Caliphs are to be chosen from the **umma**
  - **85%** of contemporary Muslims belong to the Sunni branch
- **The Shi’a faith**
  - **Ali** was the legitimate **Caliph**
  - He was also selected as Muhammad’s **spiritual** successor
  - Caliphs should be kept in Muhammad’s **family**
- Differences in their beliefs and laws developed, leading to major disputes

**The Expansion of Islam**

**Early Campaigns**

- **Conquest of the Sasanian Empire**
  - The last pre-Islamic **heir** to the **Persian Empire**
  - The campaigns saw rapid Muslim victories
  - The capital of the Sasanian Empire was taken
  - The last ruler was assassinated (**651 C.E.**)
- **Conflicts with the Byzantine Empire**
  - The Byzantine Empire was weakened by **overexpansion**
  - The Muslims were **supreme** in military power, especially in the **Mediterranean**
  - Some Byzantine **Christians** also supported Muslim advances, due to their **lower taxes**
  - Arab armies forced Byzantine authority to withdraw from **Egypt** and **North Africa (642 C.E.)**

**The Umayyad Caliphate (661-750 C.E.)**

- Moved the capital from Medina to **Damascus**
- The first Umayyad Caliph was **Muawiya**
- Conquered areas through militaristic **expansion**
- **Administration**
  - Huge **bureaucracy**
  - Treatment of **Dhimmi**, or non-Muslims
    - required the payment of **jizya**, a tax
    - tolerance
    - **“People of the Book”** (Jews & Christians) were treated better
  - Treatment of Muslim Arabs
    - **first-class citizens**
    - paid lower taxes
    - could join the imperial administration & army
    - had a share of riches from conquest
  - Converts to Islam (sing. **Mawal**) were seen as **inferior** to born Muslims
- **Decline**
  - **Decentralized** bureaucracy; the structure became almost **tribal**
  - **Religious tension** between the Sunni & Shi’a
  - Non-Arab **converts** to Islam sought more **rights**

**The Golden Age of Islam**

**The Abbasid Caliphate** **(750-1258 C.E.)**

- **The Abbasid Revolution**
  - The luxurious lifestyles of the Umayyad Caliphs caused discontentment and unrest.
  - Frontier warriors of the **Abbasid** party allied with the **Shi’a** and **non-Arab** Muslims to revolt (747 C.E.)
  - The Abbasids won the **Battle of the Zab**; they quickly conquered the rest of the Empire (750 C.E.)
  - **Abu al Abbas** became Caliph.
  - The **Umayyads** were **massacred** at a “reconciliation dinner”; a survivor, **Abu al-Rahman I**, fled to the Iberian Peninsula to found the **Cordoba Caliphate.**
- **The Golden Age of Islam**
  - **Baghdad** became the center of world **trade** and **education.**
  - The Caliphate faced **political decline** and **social turmoil.**
  - **Cultural vibrance** persisted, and by the 12th century, schools, libraries, and institutes flourished in **Cairo** and **Baghdad.**
- **International Trade**
  - Built a vast **trading network**, covering products from the **Silk Roads.**
  - **Technology**, **knowledge**, and **culture** **exchanges** occurred (e.g. the Indo-Arabic numerals were a result of this).
  - Bank & **economic structures** were **complexified**: the concepts of partnership and credit were introduced.
- **Islamic Literature & Art**
  - **Persian**: considered the language of “high culture”.
    - **Rubaiyat** by Omar Khayyam: a collection of poems.
    - **Shahnameh** (Book of Kings) by Ferdowsi: an epic poem depicting myths of the Persian Empire.
  - **Arabic**: the language of **religion**, **law**, and **natural sciences.**
  - **Calligraphy** & **illustrated poetry** featured themes such as desert journeys, chivalry, romance, etc.
  - **Architecture** advancements manifested in the construction of minarets and mosques.
- **Agriculture**
  - The caliphate covered a wide **variety** of land, and, hence, climates.
  - Massive and advanced **irrigation projects** were carried out to accommodate the needs of the new variety of crops.
  - Hydropower and windmills eased work and increased production.
- **Learning**
  - Scholars **translated** **Greco-Roman** and **Indian** books into Arabic, preserving and building upon knowledge in a variety of fields.
  - Advanced in algebra, geometry, medicine, anatomy, and ethics.
  - **Medicine**
    - Had hospitals and the best healthcare of the time.
    - Passing a test was a required prerequisite to becoming a physician/pharmacist.
    - The eye surgery that removes **cataracts** was developed.
- **Roles of Women**
  - Became **increasingly subjugated** to men.
  - Eventually required to wear veils and cover their bodies fully.
  - Lived increasingly **secluded lives.**
  - The mothers of Caliphs were the most prominent.
  - Wealthy women were restricted to the home & were often married off early.
  - Lower-class women worked.
  - The number of slaves & **concubines** increased with wealth.
    - Concubines were often better off than wives, being usually educated and able to participate in public life.

**The Cordoba Caliphate (756-1031 C.E.)**

- Founded by **Abu al-Rahman**, a **Umayyad** survivor who fled to the **Iberian Peninsula.**
- Located in **Al-Andalus.**
- The Muslim **Moors**, comprising Berbers and North African Muslims, expanded into the Iberian Peninsula and Europe (711 C.E.)
  - Their conquest was halted by Christian kings at the **Battle of Tours** in France (732 C.E.)
- Scholars in the Cordoba Caliphate preserved **Greco-Roman** knowledge.
- Fostered by policies of **tolerance**, a unique **Spanish-Arabic** style emerged in art, vocabulary, and architecture.
- **Cordoba** became another major ancient center of **learning.**

**African Civilizations**

**Axum and Kush**

**Kush**

- Emerged in South of Egypt in **Nubia** by the end of the second millennium B.C.E.
- Established a new capital at **Meroe.**
- Meroe became a trading hub for **iron** goods.

**Axum**

- Located in **Ethiopia.**
- Came to power in the **third century C.E.**
- **Trade**
  - Located in 2 main cities: **Adulis** & **Axum.**
  - Goods & slaves were traded through **ports** on the Red Sea.
  - Exported ivory, hides, and gold.
  - Competed for control of the **ivory trade** with Meroe.
- **Religion in Early Axum**
  - **Monotheistic** with Animist beliefs.
  - Believed that kings were descended from God.
  - Honored dead ancestors.
- **Conversion to Christianity**
  - Christianity was first introduced through trade in the 300s C.E.
  - **King Ezana** made Christianity the **official religion.**
  - Conversion to Christianity initially **strengthened ties** in **trade.**
  - Axum remained Christian **after Islam** was introduced to Africa in the 600s C.E.
  - This eventually led to conflict in the twelfth century C.E.
- **King Ezana** **(325-360 C.E.)**
  - Conquered Meroe, creating an **Axum empire.**
  - Converted Axum to **Christianity.**
- **Axum culture**
  - Blended the traditions of **Arabs** and **Kushites.**
  - The Adulis population comprised Egyptians, Arabs, Greeks, Romans, Persians, and Indians.
  - **Greek** was the international language.
- **Axumite innovations**
  - Developed a **writing system**: “Ge’ez”.
  - Became the only ancient African kingdom to have a written language besides Egypt and Meroe.
  - **Minted coins** in bronze, silver, and gold; became the first sub-Saharan state to do so.
  - Developed terrace farming.
  - Employed canals and dams for irrigation.
- **Pillars of Axum**
  - Constructed **tall pillars** made from solid granite as monuments/tomb markers.
  - Recorded achievements on them.
  - **Stelae**: **exploits** recorded on stone pillars.

**East Africa**

**Coastal trade centers**

- **Indian Ocean Trade**
  - Preferred due to **lower transportation costs.**
  - Carried more **bulk** & **staple** goods, compared to the Silk Road, which carried more luxury items.
  - African exports: **raw materials**, such as furs, ivory, gold, salt, and timber.
  - African imports: Indian, Islamic, and Chinese **luxuries.**
  - **Monsoons**, or alternating wind currents, aided transportation.
  - Trade occurred between **decentralized**, individual merchant towns.
- **Coastal trade centers develop**
  - City-states formed by gatherings initiated by trade.
  - Kilwa, Sofala, and Mogadishu were major centers.
- **Swahili culture** **(12th** **& 13th** **centuries C.E.)**
  - International trade led to cultural diffusion and **integration.**
  - **Swahili** (Arabic for “of the coast”) culture: a **cosmopolitan** culture that involves a mixture of **African** and **Arabic** cultures.
  - Swahili language: a blend of **Bantu** and **Arabic** languages; originated as a **Pidgin** for trade, then evolved into a **Creole** and mature language.

**Great Zimbabwe** **(900s-1500s C.E.)**

- An **inland capital** of **trade.**
- “Zimbabwe” in Bantu means “stone houses”.
- The city consisted of **stone edifices**, constructed without mortar.
- Built and occupied by the **Bantu** peoples.
- Reached its height of prosperity (around 1300 C.E.)
- **Artifact evidence indicates:**
  - **International trade.**
  - A likely **monarchical** government.
- **Decline** **(1500s C.E.)**
  - **Overpopulation**, **Civil war**, and **Dwindling trade.**
  - Depleted resources, and, thus, a shift of **gold** production and trade further into the **interior.**

**West Africa**

**Ghana** **(300s-1235 C.E.)**

- First **great trading state** in West Africa.
- Formed by the **Soninke** people in 300s C.E..
- Located in the **upper Niger River valley**; comprised grasslands.
- **Lifestyle**
  - Skilled **iron-makers.**
  - Had an **agricultural** economy of separate villages under **local rulers.**
- **Trade patterns**
  - Traded across the **Sahara** via **Berbers** on camel caravans.
  - **Camels** “fleets of the desert”.
  - **Exported**: **gold**, iron, ivory, ostrich feathers, hides, and slaves.
  - **Imported**: **salt**, textiles, horses.
- **Politics**
  - Ghana kings
    - Acted as **war leaders.**
    - Negotiated **trade** with foreigners.
    - Governed without written laws.
  - Powerful and large armies
    - The Ghanaians were **expansionists** who conquered more territory.
- Reached **peak** of its power (1050 C.E.)
- **Tunka Manin**, Ghana’s most powerful ruler, commanded a 200,000 men army (1067 C.E.)
- Began to decline in 1000s C.E.
- **Berbers** invaded and destroyed the city of **Kumi Saleh** (1076 C.E.)
- Soninke lost control of the salt trade to neighboring tribes.
- The **Malinke** people overthrew Ghana and established the Empire of **Mali** **(1235 C.E.)**

**Mali**

- **Sundiata Keitu**
  - **Founded** the Empire of Mali.
  - Defeated the **Ghanaians** (1240 C.E.)
  - United the Malians under a **strong government.**
  - Regarded as the father of his nation.
- Territory included part of the **Atlantic coast** and ran east to the city of **Timbuktu.**
- Built its wealth and power on the **gold-salt trade.**
- Most of its citizens were farmers who were ruled by local authorities that answered to the Malian king.
- Reached the peak of its power under **Mansa Musa** (1312-1337 C.E.)
  - **Doubled** the size of Mali.
  - Had a strong, centralized government.
  - Governed the kingdom by dividing it into provinces.
  - Was a **devout Muslim**
    - Traversed to Mecca on a famous **pilgrimage.**
    - Was lavishly generous with gold, so much so that he caused inflation.
    - Demonstrated his great power and wealth as well as his kingdom’s.
    - Absorbed new ideas about Islamic learning & architecture.
  - **Timbuktu** became the center of Islamic learning & culture.
- Divided by **civil war** (1349 C.E.)
- Supplanted by **Songhai** rule within 100 years.

**Ibn Battuta**

- **Moroccan**-born **traveler** & explorer.
- Traveled through the **Islamic world,** from North Africa to China (1325-1354 C.E.)
- His writings were valuable **primary sources** about the Islamic world in Africa.

**Songhai**

- Songhai culture developed **east of Timbuktu**, along the **Niger River.**
- **King Kossi** establishes the **Dia dynasty** (1009 C.E.)
  - Converts to **Islam**
  - The kingdom benefited from **Muslim trade routes**
- **Sunni Ali** founds another dynasty, the **Sunni** (1464 C.E.)
  - The dynasty expanded to include **Timbuktu & Djenne.**
  - Established control over the **trading empire.**
  - Maintained the **existing** trade patterns.
- **Askia Muhammad** (also called **Muhammad Ture**) overthrew Sunni Ali’s son (1493 C.E.)
  - Continued policy of **expansion**, maintaining power through a navy and cavalry.
  - Established a **complex government** centered in **Gao.**
  - Home to many great centers of **learning.**

**Influence of Islam in West Africa**

- Provided **universal faith**, **sense of community**, and a **powerful political/legal system.**
- **Royal Cult**
  - Defined to be the religious/quasi-religious veneration of a monarch.
  - Rulers **reinforced authority** through Muslim ideology.
  - Monarchs established themselves as **spiritual** and **political** leaders.
- Many Africans exposed to Islam also retain their **indigenous** religion.
- Myriad **Sudanic matrilineal** societies were **hesitant** to convert to Islam, as it **restricted women** more than these societies did.
- **Intraregional Trade**
  - The **slave trade**, which had existed since Classical times, was **globalized** by Islam.
  - Slavery & the slave trade grew in scale and **prominence**, with **7 million** slaves traded.
- The majority of Africa **remained isolated** from larger networks even after the introduction of Islam.

**Middle Ages**

**Definitions and Periods**

- **Classical Civilization** (**Greek** and **Roman**)
- **Middle Ages** (**Fall of Rome** to the **Renaissance**)
  - **Early Middle Ages** (500–1000 C.E.)
  - **High Middle Ages** (1000-1350 C.E.)
  - **Late Middle Ages** (1350-1500~ C.E.)
- **Modern Times** (**Scientific Revolution** to today)

**"The Dark Ages"**

- **Fall of Rome** to the **Renaissance**
- Implies a time of **oppression**, lack of **culture**, and lack of **creativity**.

**The Fall of Rome**

- A time of **Germanic** tribes and people groups: **Germani**, **Alemanni** (who styled themselves "**Theut**"), **Franks**, and **Vandals**.
- **Goths** were considered less "problematic" because they were more **Romanized**.
- Resulted in the **disruption of trade**, a **shift in education**, a **language shift**, and a **cultural shift** toward **Germanic** traditions.

**Germanic Culture and Society**

- **Clans**: Consisted of up to 50 related households.
- **Feud**: **Blood vengeance** taken on rival clans; **Germanic law** was designed to stop blood feuds.
- **Wergild (Compensation)**: Money paid to end a feud; the amount was dependent on the **importance of the person**.
- **Raiding**: Acted as an annual income supplement in some cases.
- **Chief**: A great military leader elected by clan leaders.

**Trial by Ordeal**

- Methods included **hot iron**, **hot water**, **cold water**, and **judicial combat**.

**Frankish Kingdoms**

**Clovis (481–511** **C.E.)**

- **Frankish King** of the **Merovingian Dynasty**.
- A shrewd strategist and warrior.
- Established the era of the **"Long-Haired Kings."**
- Converted to **Christianity**.
- Conquered **Alaric II** and the **Visigoths**.
- Intermarried with the **Gallo-Romans**.
- Allied with the **Christian Clergy**.
- Established the capital at **Paris**.

**The Merovingians (457–751** **C.E.)**

- Known as the **"Long-Haired Kings"** and **Warriors**.
- Characterized by **plundered land**, **fratricide**, and frequent **civil war**.
- **"Mayors of the Palace"** gained authority while kings lost it.
- **Charles "The Hammer" Martel** (718–741 C.E.):
  - Served as the **Mayor of the Palace**.
  - Champion of **Christianity** and a French hero.
  - Led the **Battle of Tours**; while sometimes overblown as the sole cause for the end of Muslim expansion in Europe, it marks a significant endpoint.
  - Extended **Frankish control** to the south.

**Pepin the Short (751–768** **C.E.)**

- Overthrew the **Merovingian** line.
- Crowned by the **Pope** as the **"Protector."**
- Defeated the **Lombards** who were threatening Rome—this led to the **Donation of Pepin**.
- Crystallized the **alliance** between the **Pope (Stephen III)**, the **Mayor**, and the **Missionaries**.
- Established the **Carolingian Dynasty**.

**The Carolingian Dynasty (751–987** **C.E.)**

- **Charlemagne (742–814** **C.E.)**:
  - Son of Pepin and the most powerful **Carolingian**.
  - Founder of **"Europe"** by merging **Christian**, **Roman**, and **German** elements to politically unite West and Central Europe.
  - First **Emperor** in 325 years (crowned in the year 800).
  - Led a **revival** and **renaissance** in **education**, **culture**, and **unification**.
- **Administration**:
  - Divided into 300 counties.
  - **Count**: The King's local representative in law and finance.
  - **Duke**: The King's local military official.
  - **Baron**: Lesser lords of smaller estates.
  - **Office**: A conferred position of authority to act for the **public good**.

**Monasticism**

**A Way of Life**

- Involved renouncing **worldly pursuits** and taking vows of **poverty**, **chastity**, and **obedience**.
- Followers lived by a **Rule**—a life dedicated to God.
- Despite leaders like Charlemagne, **monks** were the primary **missionaries** from 500 to 1100 Common Era.

**Monasteries**

- **Monasteries** appeared as a response to the perceived **worldliness** of the church.
- Commissioned for purposes of **education** and the **well-being** of the general population.
- **Functions**:
  - **Religious studies**, **schooling**, local **economies**, providing **lodging and food**, and helping the poor.
- **Monks preserved knowledge**:
  - They preserved and added to **Classical texts** and the writings of the **Church Fathers**.
- **Scriptorium (Libraries)**: Places of vast knowledge where texts were copied (for example, it took two scribes one year to copy one Bible).
- Provided **standardized education**.

**The Liberal Arts**

- Considered essential for a **free person**.
- Goal: To produce **virtuous**, **knowledgeable**, and **articulate** people able to participate in **civic and religious life**.
- Divided into the **Trivium** and the **Quadrivium**.
- **The Quadrivium**:
  - **Arithmetic**: For trade and industry.
  - **Astronomy**: For navigation and seasons.
  - **Geometry**: For logic and construction.
  - **Music**.
- Provided **specialized skills** and **higher education**.
- Students learned **theology**, **philosophy**, and **medicine**
- Earned degrees such as **Baccalaureates**, **Masters of Arts**, and **Doctors**.

**The Church in Medieval Life**

**The Church as the Center of Life**

- Involved in everything from **birth (Baptism)** to **death (Last Rites)**.
- **Local Saints**:
  - **Patrons** to be honored and prayed to; they gave specific areas prestige.
- **Parish Priests** managed local spiritual life.
- **The Mass**:
  - The center of life, viewed as necessary for **salvation** and the stability of society.

**Carolingian Decline**

**The Decline of the Empire**

- No lasting empire was maintained **post-mortem** (after death).
- **Partible Inheritance**:
  - **Louis the Pious**, son of Charlemagne, divided his kingdom among his three sons: **Louis the German**, **Lothar**, and **Charles the Bald**.
- **Competition**:
  - Multiple German and Italian kings began calling themselves **"Holy Roman Emperors."**
  - **Local lords** held the majority of power in Germany, and **city-states** re-emerged in Italy.
- **Bureaucracy** was not yet strong enough to maintain unity.
- Resulted in strong **cultural unity** through the church, but a **politically divided** landscape.

**Carolingian Successors**

- **West Francia** was ruled by the **Capetian Dynasty** (**987 to 1328** **C.E.)**
- They slowly **consolidated royal power** and built a central **administration**.
- **East Francia** was ruled by the **Ottonian**, **Salian**, and **Hohenstaufen** families as **Holy Roman Emperors**.

**The Vikings** **(~790-1066 C.E.)**

**Basic Knowledge**

- **Viking** was a verb and a job description.
  - They were **explorers**, **traders**, and **warriors**.
- By the end of the era, many settled in other regions.
- Left significant **linguistic**, **cultural**, and **social impacts**.

**Kievan Rus** **& Magyars**

**Kievan Rus**

- A mix of mostly **Slavs** and **Vikings**.
- **Swedish and Danish Kings** were invited to become leaders—**Rurik** is the most famous.
- Created **trading settlements**, including **Kiev** and **Novgorod**.
- Modelled their society based on the **Byzantines**.
- **Aristocrats (Boyars)** held less power than in other regions.
- **Peasants** were mostly **free farmers**.
- Known for **ornate churches**, highly religious **literature** and **art**, and a strong **monastic movement**.

**Magyars**

- **Semi-nomadic Hunnic peoples** who periodically raided and invaded Southeastern and Central Europe in the 9th and early 10th centuries.
- The **Ottonian Kings** of the East Franks slowly halted these invasions.

**The Great Schism**

- The **permanent split** between the **Orthodox Church** and the **Latin Church**.
- Resulted from **papal claims of supremacy**, accusations of **idolatry**, and the **Filioque Controversy**.
- **Filioque Controversy**: A dispute over whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the **Father and the Son (Latin)** or from the **Father alone (Greek)**.

**Feudalism and Manorialism**

- **Feudalism**: A system of **political and military obligations** that bound **Lords** and their **Retainers**.
- **Manorialism**: A system of **economic and social relationships** between **Landlords** and their **Peasant laborers**.

**Nobility**

- A **hereditary ruling class**.
- The **first-born male** typically inherits the estate (**primogeniture**).
- Other children often became members of the **Clergy**, **political leaders**, or **Knights**.
- Noblemen were given a **fief (estate)** by the King
- Expected to pay **taxes** and provide **soldiers**.
- On a **fief**, the **Lord's word is law**.

**Knights**

- **Mounted soldiers**
- Usually owed 40 days of military service per year.
- Responsibilities included **guard duty**, attending **court**
- Given **land** and **prestige** in return.
- **The Code of Chivalry**:
  - **Prowess**: Excellence with the sword and horse; never laying down arms.
  - **Courage**: Being brave (but not foolhardy) and protecting the weak.
  - **Generosity**: Practicing hospitality and showing mercy to those who ask.
  - **Loyalty**: To the Lord, the King, and the Church.
- Reality was not always **chivalrous**:
  - When bored, some would **raid villages**, **pillage**, and commit acts of violence.
  - The Church and some Kings looked to **reduce knights' violence** through the **Crusades**, the **Code of Chivalry**, and **tournaments**.

**Peasantry**

- **Freemen / Freeholders**:
  - Owned their own land
  - Contributed **labor**, **crops**, and **taxes** to the Lord.
- **Serfs / Villeins**:
  - **Landless peasants** who were tied to the Lord's land.
  - Lived a simple but **protected life**.
  - Could not be **bought or sold** (they were not slaves).
  - Could **pass on property** and rights through inheritance.
  - Were generally left alone if they **met their obligations**.

Pre-Capitalist Society

- The system was underpinned by **generational and personal loyalty**, **services** **for protection**, **religious devotion**, **honor**, and **tradition**.

markdown:
# S2M-1 Semester 2 Midterm review: Mongols, Late Medieval + Renaissance Europe

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Midterm History H review guide (PA). Writers: James Gao 9-6, Sunny Jin 9-1. Editor: Aiden Chen 9-12. Range: Mongols, Late Medieval + Renaissance Europe. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Mongols**

**Who were they?**

- Group of nomadic people that came from the steppes
- Steppes: vast, dry treeless grasslands stretching across Eurasia; semi-arid and ideal for nomadic herding and horseback warfare
- Steppes are modern day Mongolia, Southern Russia including Kazakhstan, and around
- Tribes in the steppe combined and grouped together by the Genghis Khan in 1206
- Genghis Khan’s tribe: Khamag mongols –confederation of 38 clans
- Genghis Khan: Originial name is Temujin
- Genghis Khan translated to English is “Universal Ruler”

Accomplishments

- Built the largest land empire in history, stretching from East Asia to Eastern Europe (larger compared to Alexander the Great or Napoleon)
- Developed an organized decimal military system (groups of 10, 100, 1000…)
- Brought political stability to much of Eurasia, known as the Pax Mongolica: peace in Mongolia
- Advanced warfare with short bows, cavalry tactics, and siege engineering
- Laid the foundation for Mongol-ruled states like China’s **Yuan Dynasty** and Golden Horde.

**Characteristics of Mongolian society**

- Strong focus on family, loyalty, and hierarchy
- Men skilled in horse riding, archery, and warfare
- Women managed herds, homes, and often trade, money and economics
- Highly mobile, adaptable to harsh steppe climate
- Little fixed agriculture; relied on animals for food
- Strong oral tradition of stories and poetry
- Meritocratic: Positions based on strength and ability, not birth
- Not oppressive rule
- Respected scholars, artists, and artisans

**Mongolian Religion**

- Tengrism: centered on Tengri (the Eternal Blue Sky). It was worshipped with animism, shamanism, ancestor reverence, and nature harmony
- Later developed religious tolerance/interfaith (unlike European societies: Jewish people hated for not believing in Jesus)

**Military Campaigns**

- Mongol invasion of Eastern Europe: 1237–1242
- Europe at the time: Middle Ages
  - Feudal kingdoms (France, England, Holy Roman Empire)
  - Crusades still ongoing
  - Dominated by knights, castles, and the Catholic Church
  - Mongols unknowingly brought black death to Europe
- They stopped the invasion of Europe because of the death of Ögedei Khan (son of Genghis Khan)
- Genghis Khan never reached Europe — his conquests were all in Asia
- Customs forced them to go back to their capital after Khan died to reelect: Karakorum ceremonial purposes and respect for religion and Khan
- Mongols were organized and mobilized for war at all times

**Economic characteristics**

- Increased trade
- Unified the entire Silk Road under one empire
- Established the **yam (post station)** system for travel and communication.
- Issued **passports (paiza)** for merchants, which guaranteed protection across territories. Demanded goods from conquered populations and land
- Protected merchant caravans with military patrols.
- **Ortogh System**: Mongolian government funded association to support and promote caravans in trade, merchants; ensured safety and prevented banditrobbing
- Welcomed traders of all religions and ethnicities with tolerance
- Built and maintained roads, bridges, and supply depots
- Connected Europe, the Middle East, and Asia in a single safe trading zone
- Diplomatic immunity: Mongols protected and respected messengers because of the ability to build relations and connect countries
- Killing a messenger was threatening war
- A Russian prince did this and was crushed by Mongols
- Religious tolerance – For purposes of strengthening country
- SAQs – Some lands payed taxes to Mongols, but not under Mongol rule
- An example is a part of Russia. Moscow payed taxes for weaker states and combined them, eventually defeating the Golden Horde.

**Accomplishments (Politically/socially)**

- **Khubi System**: gifted lands, shares, and other spoils of war to family and loyal companions largely within a common origin.
- **Yasa code**: forbids lies, thefts, adultery…
- Ata – Malik Juvayni: every crime had specific penalty and consequences
- Reforms of Mongke Khan
- Agricultural workers had safety from taxes and excessive obligations to landowners
- Rich payed more while poor payed less
- Government welfare helped poor

**Fall of the Mongol empire**

- **Genghis Khan** (1206–1227)
- **Ögedei Khan** (1229–1241)
- **Güyük Khan** (1246–1248)
- **Möngke Khan** (1251–1259)
- After the death of Genghis Khan, his sons fought over territory
- After the death of Mongke Khan, the empire broke down in to 4 khanates
- Golden Horde (Russia and eastern Europe)
- Yuan dynasty (China and Mongolia)
- Chagatai Khanate (Central Asia)
- Ilkhanate (Persia and the Middle east)

**Chagatai Khanate**

- Lead by Chagatai Khan (son of Chinggis Khan)
- Became increasing decentralized into sub-Khanates

**Golden Horde**

- 1237-1238 CE: Mongol forces invaded Russia (which was unable to defend due to its division into many small kingdoms)
- Religious tolerance of Orthodox church
- Increased Eurasian trade
- High taxes on peasants
- Russia isolated from Western European commercial and cultural influence
- Russians defeated the Golden Horde in 1380 CE

**Ilkhanate**

- 1258 captured Baghdad, killed Abbasid caliph
- Used local lords to administer taxes, tribute, and census taking
- Tolerant of scholars and artisans
- Assimilated Middle-Eastern values
- Reinvigorated Eurasian trade routes

**Yuan Dynasty**

- Kublai Khan toppled Song in 1279
- Tried to prevent Mongols from being absorbed into Chinese civilization
- Reserved highest government jobs for Mongols and non-Chinese officials
- Religiously tolerant

**Black Death**

**Causes**

- widely believed to be a result of the plague caused by infection with the bacterium Yersinia pestis
- spread by fleas on rats, then human to human
- originated in China and Central Asia in the mid-1300s. It was transmitted to Crimea in 1347 by Mongol armies
- from Crimea, it spread to other ports in Europe through **trade ships**, and was also spread by merchants on trade routes
- germ theory and microbes did not exist yet

**Immediate Reactions**

- devout, pre-scientific people struggled to understand what was happening
- some saw it as **divine punishment**
  - flagellants would whip themselves to seek forgiveness from God
  - others prayed to God for an end to the plague, seeking divine mercy
- people were quarantined for 40 days in attempts to prevent the spread of the plague
- trade and wars were disrupted
- rise in anti-semitism as Jews were blamed; pogroms and violence against Jewish communities increased
- there was also persecution of other groups such as foreigners, pilgrims, and the poor

**Long Term Consequences**

- roughly one third of Europe's population died
- due to high mortality, there was a shortage of workers, so workers demanded better pay and better conditions
- fewer workers meant less agricultural land was cultivated
- there was a loss of faith as people blamed God for the plague
- generally weakened Feudalism and "brought a new fluidity to the thirteenth century"
- there was a breakdown of social structure, and lord/vassal relationships ended
- art focused on mortality and afterlife

**Renaissance**

**Some Earlier Renaissances**

- **Carolingian Renaissance**: 8th to 9th centuries
  - monastic learning, much circulation of Latin literature (both old and new)
- **Macedonian Renaissance**:
  - 10th century, mostly artistic developments
  - more "realistic" painting, early use of simple perspective
- **12th century Renaissance**
  - Thomas Aquinas, Hildegard von Bingen, numerous other scholastic philosophers and theologians

**Contributing Factors**

- Italian city-states increasing trade
- decline of Catholic church political power, rise of city-states and national monarchies
- increase in trade, economic growth, knowledge of world, banking
- **cultural diffusion** (across Europe and the world)
- more social mobility and economic opportunities

**Economic causes**

- wealth from crusades and Mediterranean trade routes
- Hanseatic League (mostly northern Europe)
- economic opportunities after Black Death
- growth of banking

**Italian City-States Trade Dominance**

- breakup of Mongol Empire(s) led to decline of Silk Roads
- rise of Ottoman empire led to change in trade patterns (possibly the decline in some routes)

**Why** **the** **Renaissance began in Italy**

- banking and international trade led to great wealth
- higher levels of urbanization and wealth
- it was the previous center of classical civilization (Roman empire)
- incredibly wealthy benefactors (Medici family) were able to fund artists to justify their wealth and for their family's prestige
- early example of **philanthropy** (ultra rich using their wealth to create art, resources, and fairs for the general public)

**Renaissance Culture**

- deep roots in medieval traditions and cultural development
- not a rejection of religion, not secularism
  - religion deeply present in much Renaissance art and culture in general
- not modern or contemporary individualism
  - community life still critically important

**Humanism**

- in Antiquity, art focused on mythical heroes and kings (Hercules, Achilles, Alexander the Great, etc.)
- in the Middle Ages, art tended to focus on the explicitly religious: God, Jesus, angels, demons, saints, etc.
- **Humanism** is the belief in the value of human life, humanistic values, and experiences, and that it evolved so that even a regular human life is worthy of art and reflection
- **Petrarch**-Florentine scholar
- Wrote of “Three Ages”: Classical, Dark, Golden
- Encouraged Europeans to read classical literature
- in the Middle Ages, the body was seen as a sinful vessel; the body was worthy of analysis in Humanism
- the study of the humanities was influenced by ancient Greece and Rome, which encouraged reading the "classics"
- emphasized human nature
- the founders of Humanism were Christian; the movement was not anti-Christian

**Ideas in Humanism**

- The study of humanities and classical culture
- Individual improvement
- Action rather than passivity
- The use of reason to improve worldly conditions
- Observe lessons of nature
- Fascination with physical form

**Political Aspect**

- Debated characteristics of ideal rulers and ideal forms of government\

**Artistic Aspects**

- Religious symbolism
- Realism and human emphasis in religion
- Linear perspective
- Heavy classical influence

**Spread of the Renaissance**

- Spread by merchants, scholars, bakers, and the elite
- Gutenberg’s printing press contributed
- Growing trade due to wealthy patrons

markdown:
# S2F-1 Semester 2 Final review: Reformation, Age of Exploration, Civilizations of the Americas

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Final History H review guide (PA). Writers: Cherie 9-10, Wyeth 9-10. Editor: Sunny 9-1. Range: Reformation, Age of Exploration, Civilizations of the Americas. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**15 Europe Transformed: Reform and State-Building**

**The Reformation of the Sixteenth Century**

- Protestant Reformation: a religious reform movement that divided the western church into Catholic and Protestant groups
  - Begin with Martin Luther

**Background to the Reformation**

- 15th century late: attempt to reestablish the centralized power of monarchical governments
  - Known as ‘Renaissance states’ / ‘new monarchies’ -> France, England, Spain
- New Renaissance monarchs: crafty men obsessed with acquisition and expansion
  - Concentration of royal authority
  - Attempts to suppress nobility
  - Efforts to control the church are in their hands
  - Obtain a new source of revenue -> increase royal power & military
- Niccolò Machiavelli -> The Prince (1513)
  - Middle age: many political theorists stressed the ethical side of the prince
    - Based on the Christian moral principles
  - Machiavelli: abandon morality as the basis for the analysis of political activity
    - Emphasize reaching the results regardless of the methods employed
- Trade increased after previous economic recessions in the 14th century
  - Society was separated into 3 estates (Mainly in the Middle Ages, some in now)
- Clergy -> First Estate
- Nobility -> Second Estate
- Peasants and inhabitants -> Third estate
- Nobles (2~3% of population) -> declining real incomes
  - Some old Nobles survived, but new ones also came
  - Still dominated society and held important political posts and was an advisor
- Peasants (85~90% of Third Estate), except in the urban areas of Flanders and northern Italy
  - Serfdom decreased as labor dues owned soon became rent paid in money
  - 1500s: More peasants became legally free
    - They also grew to resent their social superiors
    - Fought for a greater share of the benefits coming from labor
    - This led to a peasant revolution in Germany in the 1500s
- Inhabitants (10~15% of the Third Estate):
  - Originally, only artisans and merchants
  - 1500s-> Top of the urban society: Patricians
    - Wealth from capitalistic enterprises in trade, industry, and banks
    - Dominate urban community economically, socially, and politically
  - > Second level: Petty burghers
    - Shopkeepers, artisans, guild masters, guildsmen
    - Concerned with providing goods and services for locals
  - > Third level: propertyless workers (30~40% of urban inhabitants)
    - Pitiful wages/ unemployed -> miserable lives
    - Led them to radical religious reforms by the 1500s
- Printing development
  - 1100s: printing on hand-carved wooden blocks
  - 1400s: multiple printing with movable metal type
    - A gradual process that culminated sometime between 1445 and 1450
- Johannes Gutenberg of Mainz played an important role
  - Gutenberg’s Bible -> first true book under movable type
  - 1500s: a thousand printers in Europe (8~10 million copies)
- Encouraged scholarly research & lay reading in public
  - New religious ideas of the Reformation spread
  - Allowed European cultures to compete with Eastern civilizations
- Christian Humanism / Northern Renaissance Humanism since 1550s+
  - Believed in the ability of humans to reason & improve through classical texts
  - Whilst still having an inner piety towards Christianity
  - Believed that to change society, they must first change humans
  - Begin with Desiderius Erasmus:
    - Formulated and popularized Christian humanism
    - Named it ‘philosophy of Christ.’
      - Christianity should be a guiding philosophy for daily life instead of the medieval practices
      - Laid the road for the Lutheran Reformation
- Corruption leads to reform
  - 1450~1520: Renaissance popes failed to meet the church’s needs
  - Supposed to be spiritual leaders, yet involved themselves in worldly concerns
    - Julius II led armies against enemies -> denounced by pious Christians
  - Many high church officials regard their office as an opportunity to gain wealth
    - Others are ignorant of their spiritual duties
- Ordinary ppl was clamoring for meaningful religious expression & salvation
  - Some salvation processes became almost mechanical
  - Many people used relics (bones/ other objects associated with saints)
    - Frederick the Wise amassed nearly 19000 relics
    - People earn the right to buy indulgences by visiting relics

**Martin Luther and the Reformation in Germany**

- Martin Luther: Monk and professor at the University of Wittenberg
  - Between 1513~1516, his study of the Bible led him to question salvation
- Catholic emphasized 1. Faith 2. Good works
  - Luther: humans could never do enough good works to merit salvation
    - Humans are not saved through God’s works but through faith in God
    - *Indulgences are considered as good work merit in the Catholic POV*
    - This is the primary doctrine of the Protestant Reformation
    - His doctrine arrived from the Bible -> Bible = religious truth
- Luther did not consider himself a rebel
  - But was upset by indulgence sales (e.g., Monk Johann Tetze)
  - 1517: issued the 95 theses
    - Thousands of copies quickly spread throughout Germany
  - 1521 Jan: excommunicated by the church
  - Summoned to appear before the imperial diet of Emperor Charles V(HRE)
    - Members were outraged and demanded that he be arrested
      - But Elector Frederick of Saxony defended him
- 1524: Peasants’ War erupted
  - A religious revolt that peasants looked to Luther for support
    - However, Luther is conservative on economic and social issues
    - 1525: Luther supported a German prince to suppress the peasants
      - He believed in maintaining peace and order for God
- Luther then became dependent on state authorities for the growth of the reformed church
  - Gained support from 300ish German states in the HRE
    - The ruler took control of local churches
  - The Lutheran church then became a territorial/ state church
    - Luther instituted a new religious service to replace the Catholics
    - Focused on Bible reading, preaching the word of God, and singing hymns
- The reformation is closely tied to political activity
  - Charles V ruled a vast empire -> hope to tie the empire through the Catholic Church
    - However, the HRE consists of many independent states
    - 1555-> Peace of Augsburg: Charles needed to negotiate a truce
      - Division of Christianity
      - The Lutheran and Catholic Churches have the same legal rights
      - states are free to choose between the two
      - *An individual inside the state must follow the state*
      - Thus, Christian unity was lost

**The Spread of the Protestant Reformation:**

- Switzerland Reformation: 1) Zwinglianism 2)Calvinism
  - Zwingli-> became a priest-> led reform to destroy the Catholic practice
    - Relics & images destroyed, paintings & decorations removed
    - Monasticism, pilgrimages, papal authority, etc., were all abolished
  - He wanted alliances with Luther (failed)
    - Yet is unable to agree on the interpretation of the Lord’s Supper:
      - Zwingli -> body/blood (figuratively)
      - Luther -> Body/ Figure (Literally)
  - War between Swiss Protestants & Catholics -> death of Zwingli
    - Led to the rise of Calvinism
  - John Calvin -> from France, but fled to Switzerland to escape the Catholics
    - 1536: Institutes of the Christian Religion
      - Secured his position as the leader of Protestantism
  - Calvin aligns with Luther on faith and has achieved salvation
    - But also believe in the emphasis on the absolute sovereignty of God
    - Predestination-> God predestined some ppl to be saved (the elect) and others to be damned (reprobate)
  - 1536: begin to work on the reformation of Geneva
    - Tightly organized church -> both clergy and laymen in service
    - Consistory: a special body enforcing the moral discipline
    - Citizens of Geneva were punished for singing, dancing, swearing, etc
  - Geneva became the center of Protestantism
    - Missionaries from Geneva were sent all over Europe
- The English Reformation was rooted in the politics of King Henry VIII
  - Want to divorce w/ wife 1: Catherine of Aragon (b.c. no son)
  - And want to marry Wife 2: Anne Boleyn
    - Pope: unwilling to grant divorce -> So turned to the English church court
    - England Church Court -> Allow divorce & remarriage
  - 1534: Parliament moved to break the church of England from Rome
    - Act of Supremacy: The King was the only supreme head on earth of the church of England -> Gave Henry control of everything
      - But the religious activities ppl are very similar to Catholics
- 1547: Edward VI (Henry’s Son) *Underage, so he was more of a symbol*
  - The Archbishop Cranmer inclined towards Protestant doctrines
    - Anglican/English Church -> In a more Protestant direction
    - Gave clergy the right to marry & create a new church service
- 1553: (Bloody) Mary
  - Tried to return England to Catholicism
  - Burned more than 300 Protestant heretics
  - But England became more Protestant than before

**The Social Impact of the Protestant Reformation**

- Protestantism allowed the family to be the center of human life.
  - B.c. Catholicism saw Celibacy (to stay unmarried) as holy
    - Protestantism yet allows the clergy to marry
  - Husbands are the rulers and wives are the obedient servants in the household
- Female Role: Family life is the only destiny
- Be obedient to your husband
- Bear Children (considered as the divine plan)

**The Catholic Reformation**

- The Catholic Church lost power during the 1500s -> thus, it changed to gain strength.
- This act is called the Catholic Reformation or the Counter-Reformation.
  - Catholic Reformation: Emphasize that elements of the rejuvenation of the catholic church took place even before the protestant reformation
  - Counter-Reformation: Emphasis on the reformation of the Catholic church is used to fight against the Protestant Reformation
- Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians -> Preach to the lay people
- Oratory of Divine Love -> emphasize personal spiritual development and charity
- Overall, allow the Catholic church to keep medieval traits whilst also adjusting
  - E.g., revival of monasticism
- Jesuits (Society of Jesus):
  - From Ignatius of Loyola (a Spanish noble man)
    - Absolute obedience to the papacy and the Catholic church
    - Use of education
    - Dedication to engage in ‘ conflict for God.’
  - Restored Catholicism in parts of Germany & Eastern Europe
  - Propagation of the Catholic faith among non-Christians (e.g., to Japan, China, India)
- Reformed Papacy against Corruption
- Council of Trent: intermittently from 1545~1563 for 3 major sessions
  - Bible and Church are considered equally important
  - Both faith and good works are necessary for Salvation
  - The use of Purgatory and Indulgences is strengthened
  - However, indulgence sales are banned to prevent corruption

**Europe in Crisis 1560~1650**

- [1] Religious Wars [2] Revolutions [3] Constitutional Crises [4] Economic and Social Disintegration [5] Witchcraft Craze

**Politics and the Wars of Religion in the Sixteenth Century**

- The French Wars of Religion (1562~1598)
  - Although only 7% of the total population are Huguenots (the French Calvinists), 40~50% of the nobility are Huguenots
    - Stood as a great threat to the French Monarch
  - The French Catholics and Huguenots fought for 30 years (Catholic dominance)
  - After a Henry (Huguenot) succeeded to the throne, he converted to Catholicism (Or else no one would accept him)
    - With his coronation, the war of religion ended
  - Edict of Nantes (1598) :
    - Catholicism: the official religion of France
    - Also guarantee Huguenots the right to enjoy all political privileges
- King Philip II of Spain -> strongest enforcement of Catholicism
  - Insisted on strict conformity to Catholicism to help him govern
  - His control over the Netherlands and the killing of Calvinists led to a revolt
  - 1566: Revolt led by William of Nassau
    - 1609 Twelve Years True: recognized independence
    - Laid the foundation of the modern Dutch state
  - Effect: Spain is still a great power, but dominance has shifted to England
- Queen Elizabeth solved the religious problems her sister Mary caused
  - Act of Supremacy -> Elizabeth as the supreme of the church and state
  - The church is protestant but not that extreme on Catholics
- Philip II of Spain attempted to invade Queen Elizabeth I
  - Prepared an armada (fleet of warships)
  - Yet failed to conquer

**Economic and Social Crisis**

- Decline in population in the 1650s due to War, famine, and plague
  - *Used to be an increase after the black death in the 1300s*
- 100,00+ ppl were persecuted due to witch trials
  - Common ppl are more likely to be accused of being witches
  - 75% Female; most of them are single/widowed / over 50+ years old
    - This is b.c. ppl believe Satan may turn women into witches through lust
  - The witch trials eventually declined as time went on
- Mercantilism:
  - Prosperity of a nation is measured by Gold and Silver
  - They want to reach a surplus in their balance of trade
    - High tariff on foreign goods -> reduce imports, increase exports
  - The government should grant trade monopolies and investment in industry
    - Build a canal, transportation systems, and give subsidies
  - Colonies are valuable as sources of raw materials and markets for finished goods from the central country
- In all, Mercantilism encouraged Europe’s overseas expansion
  - Led to early world trade (but the Intereurope trade is still dominant)
  - Goods that used to be only for the wealthy make their way to the normal people
- Although Capitalism starts to form, it is still an agricultural economy
  - 80% of Europeans work on land
  - Though serfdom disappeared, the quality of life stayed similar

**Seventeenth-Century crises: Revolution and War**

- Thirty Years’ War (1618~1648):
  - HRE due to the struggle between Catholics and Protestants
  - Then Denmark, Sweden, France, and Spain joined the war due to political incentives
    - But most of the Battles were fought on German soil
  - Peace of Westphalia:
    - Proclaimed that all German states are free to determine their own religion
    - This led the HRE to lose unity and dominance
      - *Dutch Independence*
    - France became the dominant nation in return
    - Reveal that political motives became the guiding force in public affairs
- Military Power became increasingly important
  - Pressure to build an effective military machine
  - Increased use of firearms and cannons
    - Greater flexibility and mobility in tactics
    - Better disciplined and better trained armies
  - Thus, to support this pressure, they increase taxes on people
    - Creation of large bureaucracies to supervise military resources
    - Growth in the power of the Governments.

**Peoples of the Americas, Exploration, Colonization, and Its Effects**

**Why Did Europeans Begin Exploring?**

**Trade and Wealth**

- Europeans wanted direct access to Asian goods:
  - Spices (pepper, cloves, cinnamon)
  - Silk
  - Porcelain
- Trade routes became more difficult after the expansion of the Ottoman Empire: the traditional trading route of the Silk Road was controlled by the Ottoman’s and travelers received high tax. The route across the Red Sea was the second option, but the entire route required going inland before moving all the cargo back onto a ship.
- Portugal and Spain wanted to bypass the Turkish Muslim’s control of the Silk Road and Italian middlemen’s hold on the Mediterranean.

**New Technology**

- Compass and astrolabe improved navigation.
- Better cartography (mapmaking).
- Portuguese developed the **caravel**, a fast, maneuverable ship capable of long ocean voyages.

**Religion**

- Europeans wanted to spread Christianity.
- Exploration was often presented as a religious mission against Muslims and non-Christians.

**Portugal Leads the Way**

**Prince Henry the Navigator**

- Lived: 1394–1460.
- Sponsored voyages along the African coast.
- Established navigation schools and funded mapmaking.
- Motivated by:
  - Scientific curiosity
  - Wealth from trade
  - Spread of Christianity

**Portuguese Expansion**

- Explored farther down the coast of Africa throughout the 1400s.
- Established trading posts rather than large colonies.
- Created a **Trading-Port Empire**.

**Important Locations**

- Madeira Islands
- Azores Islands
- West African coast
- India
- Southeast Asia

**Commercial Agriculture**

- Portuguese plantations grew:
  - Sugar
  - Tobacco
- Imported African slaves to provide labor.
- Created a plantation model later copied throughout the Americas.

**Alfonso de Albuquerque (1511)**

- Captured key ports in the Indian Ocean.
- Helped Portugal dominate trade between Europe and Asia.
- Shifted trade profits away from Muslim merchants.

**Spain Enters the Competition**

**The Royal Wedding**

**1469**

- Ferdinand of Aragon married Isabella of Castile.
- Unified much of Spain politically.

**Reconquista**

**1492**

- Spain conquered Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Iberia.
- Completion of centuries-long Christian reconquest.

**Religious Unity**

- Spain strongly promoted Catholicism.
- Jews and Muslims faced expulsion or conversion.

**Columbus and the Americas**

**Christopher Columbus**

**1492**

- Sailed west seeking a route to Asia.
- Funded by Ferdinand and Isabella.
- Reached the Caribbean instead.

**Goals**

- Gold
- Spices
- Wealth for Spain

**Result**

- Began permanent contact between Europe and the Americas.

**Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)**

- Agreement between Spain and Portugal.
- Created a Line of Demarcation.
- Spain received most of the Americas.
- Portugal received Brazil and routes around Africa.

**Major Civilizations of the Americas**

**Maya**

**Location**

- Yucatán Peninsula and Central America.

**Achievements**

- Complex writing system.
- Accurate calendars.
- Advanced mathematics including the concept of zero.
- Large city-states.

**Aztec Empire**

**Location**

- Central Mexico.

**Capital**

- Tenochtitlán.

**Characteristics**

- Military empire.
- Collected tribute from conquered peoples.
- Population estimated at over 200,000.

**Religion**

- Polytheistic.
- Practiced human sacrifice to honor gods.

**Inca Empire**

**Location**

- Andes Mountains of South America.

**Capital**

- Cusco.

**Achievements**

- Over 25,000 miles of roads.
- Terrace farming.
- Highly organized bureaucracy.
- Used quipus (knotted cords) for record keeping.

**Colonization and Conquest**

**Hernán Cortés**

**1519–1521**

- Conquered the Aztec Empire.
- Allied with Indigenous enemies of the Aztecs.
- Captured Tenochtitlán.

**Francisco Pizarro**

**1532–1533**

- Conquered the Inca Empire.
- Captured Emperor Atahualpa.
- Seized vast amounts of gold and silver.

**Effects of Colonization**

**Columbian Exchange**

**From Europe to the Americas**

- Horses
- Cattle
- Wheat
- Smallpox
- Measles

**From the Americas to Europe**

- Corn (maize)
- Potatoes
- Tomatoes
- Cacao
- Tobacco

**Disease**

**Smallpox**

- Most devastating disease.
- Indigenous peoples had no immunity.

**Impact**

- In some areas, over 90% of the population died.
- Entire communities disappeared.

**Atlantic Slave Trade**

**Why?**

- Indigenous populations declined dramatically.
- Colonists needed labor for plantations and mines.

**Result**

- Millions of Africans were forcibly transported to the Americas.
- Plantation economies expanded throughout the Atlantic World.

**Long-Term Significance**

**Economic Effects**

- Massive flow of gold and silver into Europe.
- Growth of capitalism and global trade.
- Spain became one of Europe’s wealthiest powers.

**Cultural Effects**

- Spread of Christianity.
- Spread of Spanish and Portuguese languages.
- Mixing of Indigenous, African, and European cultures.

**Historical Significance**

- Connected Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Americas into a global network.
- Marked the beginning of globalization.
- Created both enormous opportunities and devastating consequences for Indigenous peoples.

**Skillsets and Advice:**

**Historical Interpretation:**

Like English, you should try to create a very argumentative claim, such as “Although the Europeans brought new ideas and innovations to the Americas, the source shows that the the introduction of firearms had a greater impact because of evidence A”.

Writing like this gives you clear structure while impressing your teachers you should try it out!

**Source Analysis:**

Out of all the different options in HIPP, I always go with Historical Context, and based on the info of the source I choose a second one. The good thing about Historical Context is that its predictable. As long as you remember the time periods main events (EXAMPLE: Spain got unified through intermarriage, Italy and the Ottomans were filthy rich, Portugal and Spain wanna new trade route etc.) you can write about the historical context of the source. REMEMBER to explain a bit after stating the facts. (EXAMPLE: Which is why the source depicts Pueblo’s people with newly found weaponry, showcasing its massive importance). If the source is informative explaining the mortality rate and stats-based data, go with purpose, because stats are used to emphasize scale and size (EXAMPLE: the trump administration has approved ＄100 billion worth of cookies, purpose of source: emphasizes the massive budget spent, and the importance of cookies in society). If the source is about a character or a story, then choose perspective. Because like every person on the planet, every source has biases, especially when about people. Pick up details in phrasing and word choice which can really help out in that situation. Intended audience is a tough one in my opinion, but here some advice nonetheless: always incorporate purpose when talking about intended audience. The source’s intended audience is…… in order to…….

**Geography:**

Finally when reviewing for the Geography questions (I don’t have a map sorry) bear in mind that the questions are all related to the content learnt in class asking you to match 1. Description 2. Location on Map 3. Name. So when reviewing please only spend your time remembering important locations such as Hispaniola which was the first colony in the americas, or Tenochtitlan where the Aztecs built their capital city.

# S1F-1 Semester 1 Final review: ALL

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Final History S review guide (PA). Writers: Lucas Jiang 9-2; Samual Li 9-4. Editor: Rebecca. Range: ALL. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Two Golden Ages of China**

**（Tang & Song）**

This chapter focuses on the Tang dynasty and the Song dynasty, two of the most prosperous periods in Chinese history. Both dynasties were known for strong government, economic growth, and rich cultural achievements.

**I-Mind Map Content**

| 1. Key Vocabulary | Tang Dynasty |
|---|---|
|  | Tang Taizong |
|  | Tributary State |
|  | Land Reform |
|  | Song Dynasty |
|  | Gentry |
|  | Dowry |
|  | Pagoda |

|  | Events |
|  | Effects |
|  | Checkpoint: Tang Taizong |
| 3. Song Dynasty | Causes |
|  | Events |
|  | Effects |
|  | Prosperity Despite Northern Threats |
